dataset.name: Data and code for Daily and Multi-Day Extreme Rainfall Analysis Under Future Climates Using Stochastic Storm Transposition and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 Over CONUS
description: This data package provides inputs, codes, and outputs for a comprehensive analysis of projected changes in extreme precipitation across 10 regions of the continental United States, using 34 downscaled Earth System Models (ESMs) from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections, Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (NEX-GDDP-CMIP6) dataset. These models are part of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6), a coordinated climate modeling framework widely used to assess climate change impacts. The analysis applies a stochastic storm transposition method to quantify changes in extreme rainfall under two Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) climate scenarios—SSP2-4.5 (moderate emissions) and SSP5-8.5 (high emissions)—compared to historical conditions (1995–2014 vs. 2081–2100). The dataset includes rainfall depth estimates for extreme events with return periods from 2 to 500 years across multiple storm durations (1, 3, and 5 days) for each of the 10 U.S. regions. Weighted ensemble statistics are derived from individual ESM performance against historical precipitation patterns, enabling robust uncertainty quantification through both sign-based and permutation-test-based model agreement assessments. Key analyses address: (1) relative changes in extreme precipitation for each climate scenario, (2) differences between SSP scenarios (SSP5-8.5 vs. SSP2-4.5), (3) contrasts between rare and frequent events, and (4) variations between multi-day and daily storm durations. The workflow produces ensemble statistics—median, 5th, 25th, 75th, and 95th percentiles—along with model agreement metrics that identify regions and event types with robust climate change signals. The dataset includes: processed rainfall depth outputs (netCDF format) from the RainyDay Python package, ESM weights from historical performance evaluation using DayMet observations, ensemble statistics across all storm dimensions, and figures summarizing key findings.

measurementTechnique:
Data Collection and Sources
Climate Model Data: Extreme precipitation analysis utilized 34 Earth System Models (ESMs) from the NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 dataset. The dataset provides bias-corrected and downscaled daily precipitation data at 0.25° spatial resolution for three time periods: historical (1995-2014), SSP245 (2081-2100), and SSP585 (2081-2100) scenarios.
Observational Data: Historical precipitation validation used DayMet daily precipitation observations for the period 1995-2014 to evaluate ESM performance and compute model weights.
Spatial Domains: Analysis focused on ten climatically homogeneous regions across the continental United States (CONUS), defined using transposition domains that exhibit meteorological homogeneity for stochastic storm transposition applications.

Data Processing and Extreme Precipitation Analysis
Stochastic Storm Transposition: Raw daily precipitation data from each ESM was processed using the RainyDay Python package to generate rainfall depth estimates for extreme events. The methodology employed stochastic storm transposition to:
Extract storm catalogs from the climate model data
Apply spatial transposition within defined homogeneous domains
Generate synthetic extreme precipitation through resampling
Compute rainfall depths for return periods of 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 166.67, and 500 years
Storm Duration Analysis: Three accumulation periods were analyzed: 1-day, 3-day, and 5-day durations, enabling assessment of both daily and multiday extreme precipitation events.

Model Performance Evaluation and Weighting
Performance Metrics: Individual ESM performance was evaluated against DayMet observations using mean annual precipitation patterns during the historical period (1995-2014). Performance assessment followed established methodologies for climate model evaluation.
Weight Computation: Model weights were computed for each region based on historical precipitation performance, with better-performing models receiving higher weights in ensemble calculations. Weights were normalized to sum to 100% for each region.

Statistical Analysis and Ensemble Computation
Relative Change Calculation: For each ESM, region, duration, and return period, relative changes (RC) were computed as: RC = (Future - Historical) / Historical × 100%
Ensemble Statistics: Both weighted and unweighted ensemble statistics were computed, including:
Median (50th percentile)
Interquartile range (25th and 75th percentiles)
90% confidence interval (5th and 95th percentiles)
Comparative Analysis: Differences in relative changes (ΔRC) were computed for:
Scenario comparison: ΔRC = RC(SSP585) - RC(SSP245)
Event rarity: ΔRC = RC(rare events) - RC(common events)
Duration comparison: ΔRC = RC(multiday) - RC(daily)

Model Agreement Assessment
Sign-Based Agreement: Model agreement was quantified using the percentage of models agreeing on the direction of change (increase or decrease) for each variable and location.
Permutation Test-Based Agreement: Statistical significance of model agreement was assessed using permutation tests to distinguish robust climate change signals from random variability. This approach provides a more stringent assessment of model consensus by accounting for the expected level of agreement due to chance.
Weighted Agreement: Both unweighted (equal weight for all models) and weighted (performance-based weights) agreement metrics were computed to assess the sensitivity of conclusions to model performance.

Quality Assurance and Quality Control (QA/QC)
Data Integrity Checks:
Verification of complete temporal coverage for all ESMs across historical and future periods
Validation of spatial domain consistency across models
Cross-checking of return period calculations against theoretical expectations
Statistical Validation:
Verification that ensemble statistics sum to 100% where appropriate
Consistency checks between weighted and unweighted analyses
Validation of agreement metrics against expected random distributions
Reproducibility Measures:
Standardized file naming conventions for all outputs
Complete documentation of processing parameters in NetCDF metadata
Version control of analysis scripts and configuration files

Data Organization and Documentation
All processed data, intermediate results, and final statistics are organized in NetCDF format with comprehensive metadata including:
Data provenance and processing history
Variable descriptions and units
Spatial and temporal coordinate information
Processing parameters and methodology references
The complete computational workflow is documented through eight Jupyter notebooks that provide full reproducibility of the analysis from raw climate model data to final ensemble statistics and visualizations.
